reason: Crossing orbits should bring rocky planetesimals into collisions, a direct start toward growing the embryos.
expectation: I expect a collision or aggregation stage, though the collisions may also produce debris.

alternatives.reason: Breaking a layered body could provide useful material, but I chose to start with the rocky planetesimals.

effect: Repeated impacts have produced several growing embryos, so I can now build on them.
reaction: It is satisfying to see multiple embryos emerge from the collisions.
reason: Gravitational focusing should help the embryos gather more material and grow.
expectation: I expect the embryos to grow larger as gravity increases their collision rates.

alternatives.reason: Adding rocky planetesimals also seems like a direct growth route, but I want to see how gravitational focusing works.

effect: Gravitational focusing has produced a larger, strongly attracting embryo that can gather rocky fragments.
reaction: The explanation makes the accelerating growth mechanism clear.
reason: Adding rocky fragments should grow the embryo toward a young rocky world.
expectation: I expect the embryo to accrete the fragments and grow, though its precise next stage is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Adding planetesimals to the other embryos could also advance growth, but I chose to continue with the strongly attracting embryo.

effect: The embryo has become the rocky proto-Earth, ready to acquire water-bearing material.
reaction: Following one embryo into proto-Earth makes the progression concrete.
reason: Water-bearing asteroid rock directly advances the goal of a volatile-bearing young Earth.
expectation: I expect the proto-Earth to incorporate hydrated rock and gain some of its volatile inventory.

alternatives.reason: Growing another embryo also serves a goal, but I chose to finish the proto-Earth route first.

effect: Proto-Earth has acquired hydrogen-bearing material, but that does not mean it has a surface ocean; the goal remains incomplete.
reaction: The distinction between hydrated rock and an ocean is useful.
reason: Breaking the layered planetesimal may provide metal-rich fragments for proto-Earth.
expectation: I expect fragments from the body's differentiated interior, possibly including metal.

alternatives.reason: This could grow the other embryo, but I chose to pursue material for proto-Earth first.

effect: The collision exposed metal-rich core fragments that can now be added to proto-Earth.
reaction: The connection to iron meteorites is interesting.
reason: Adding the core fragments continues the proto-Earth route toward the volatile-bearing Earth goal.
expectation: I expect proto-Earth to incorporate the metal fragments and grow; the exact resulting stage is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: This should grow another embryo, but I want to finish the proto-Earth route first.

effect: The young Earth goal is complete; another rocky embryo remains to be grown.
reaction: The overlapping delivery of metal and hydrogen-bearing material makes the growth history less rigid than a simple sequence.
reason: This is the only offered combination and should advance the remaining embryo goal.
expectation: I expect the embryos to accrete rocky planetesimals and form another larger rocky body.

effect: The remaining embryo became the hypothetical Theia, completing the chapter; its exact properties remain uncertain.
reaction: The reveal gives the second embryo a clear place in the broader story.

mostWorthwhile.text: Growing the embryo through gravitational focusing was most worthwhile: it connected increasing mass to more effective accretion.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding metal fragments to proto-Earth felt less revealing as an action, although the result clarified that metal and hydrated material arrived in overlapping periods.

surprise.text: Hydrated material did not imply a cool planet or a surface ocean; impacts and heating could redistribute its hydrogen.

arbitrary.text: Adding core fragments was a plausible way to supply metal, though why that particular addition completed the volatile-bearing Earth goal was not obvious beforehand.

continue.text: Yes. Theia’s introduction makes me curious about its proposed encounter with Earth, especially given the uncertainty around the impactor.
